# Test fixtures

Seven JPEGs for `tests/unit/exif.test.ts`. They exist to exercise the reader in
`src/core/exif.ts` against bytes real software wrote, not bytes assembled to
match the parser.

**Every pixel in this directory is generated by `rebuild-fixtures.py`.** Nothing
here is third-party photography: the earlier fixtures were product photos from a
vendor image library with no licence to redistribute, so their metadata was kept
and their image content replaced with a procedural pattern authored in that
script. The repository redistributes only what it owns.

The metadata, though, is original. It is factual data — real IFD structures,
real maker notes, real byte orders, written by real firmware — and it is the
part the parser actually reads.

## The font fixture

`dejavu-subset.ttf` (about 16 KB) is not one of the JPEGs above and is not read
by `exif.test.ts`. It exists for `tests/pixel/type.spec.ts`, which has to load a
face the way a user does — a real TrueType file through the file input — rather
than assert that `FontFace` exists.

Provenance: **DejaVu Sans**, subset to the Latin letters and digits the test
types. DejaVu's licence (the Bitstream Vera licence, plus the DejaVu changes)
permits redistribution and modification. It is a *sans* on purpose: the test's
claim is that a face the user brought reaches the canvas, and a face that looks
nothing like the app's own is the clearest way to watch that happen.

Regenerate (needs Python 3 and `fontTools`, which arrives with `matplotlib` in
the same environment):

```sh
python3 scripts/make-font-fixture.py
```

That script is an authoring tool like the JPEGs' — nothing imports it and the
build does not need it.

## What is in each file

| file | EXIF bytes written by | order | what it pins |
|---|---|---|---|
| `with-exif.jpg` | **Nikon D810** firmware, frame shot 2019-12-03 11:05:13; IFD0 later re-saved by `paint.net 4.0.21` (2019-12-04 10:27:56) | `MM` big-endian | the full tag set — D810, 85 mm, f/15, 1/125, ISO 64 — and the capture-date-vs-save-date pair |
| `with-exif-le.jpg` | the **same body**, frame shot 2019-12-02 16:50:13; IFD0 `Adobe Photoshop CC 2019 (Windows)` (save 2019-12-04 10:58:26), plus a Photoshop APP13 IRB | `II` little-endian | the same values through the opposite byte order, a 7080-byte APP1 with an IFD1 thumbnail, and an APP13 segment between APP1 and the image |
| `no-exif.jpg` | none — JFIF APP0 only | — | a real JPEG with no APP1 segment at all (must read `null`) |
| `exif-no-tags.jpg` | `paint.net 4.2.16` | `MM` | an APP1 whose IFD0 holds only resolution and Software: nothing to caption, so `null` rather than a blank plate |
| `partial-date-only.jpg` | `Paint.NET v3.5.10` | `MM` | one spec tag in the whole file (`DateTime`), and the fallback to it when no capture date exists |
| `partial-exif.jpg` | **Pillow 10.3.0** | `MM` | a partial tag set (FocalLength + ShutterSpeedValue, no FNumber/ApertureValue/ISO) and an APEX `ShutterSpeedValue` stored as an unsigned RATIONAL |
| `long-exposure.jpg` | **Pillow 10.3.0** | `MM` | a 2-second exposure stored only as `ShutterSpeedValue`, an **SRATIONAL** of −1 — the signed case |

`partial-exif.jpg` and `long-exposure.jpg` are the synthesised pair, and they
are synthesised only because no rights-clean real file has their shape: across
the machine's several thousand JPEGs, none carries `FocalLength` without
`FNumber`/`ApertureValue`, and none that could be redistributed carries a
negative `ShutterSpeedValue`. Their bytes are written by Pillow's TIFF/Exif
writer — not hand-assembled — and every value in them is what the Exif spec says
a camera writes for that shape.

## Pixel provenance

The pixels in every file are a procedural pattern: a two-axis colour ramp, wide
diagonal bands, concentric rings and a thick border, quantised to eight levels
so the fixtures stay a sane size. The generator is `synth_pixels()` in
`rebuild-fixtures.py`, seeded per file. They are not photographs and must not
look like any particular photograph.

Regenerate (needs Python 3 and Pillow; built and run against 10.3.0):

```sh
python3 tests/fixtures/rebuild-fixtures.py
```

That script is an authoring tool, not part of the build: nothing imports it, it
is not in `package.json`, and the project builds, tests and ships without it.
It is deterministic and idempotent — re-running it on these files reproduces
them byte for byte — so it doubles as the record of how they were made.

## What the rebuild preserved, exactly

For the six rebuilt files, checked against the vendor originals byte by byte:

- **APP0, APP1 and APP13 are the originals.** Same marker, same length field,
  same bytes — with one exception: the embedded thumbnails. `with-exif-le.jpg`
  carries a 160×147 one twice, in APP1's IFD1 and in APP13's `0x040C` resource,
  and those two 6000-byte slots are the only bytes that changed. They now hold a
  generated image of the same dimensions, padded to the same length with zeros
  after EOI, so the offsets around them and the segment lengths are untouched.
- **The quantization tables are byte-identical** to the vendor files', so the
  compression settings are the originals'; the scan is re-encoded at the same
  dimensions and chroma subsampling.
- **The parser's output is unchanged.** Every value `readExif` returns from
  these files — camera, focal length, aperture, shutter, ISO, date, and the
  `null` answers for `no-exif.jpg` and `exif-no-tags.jpg` — is what it was
  before the rebuild.

The one thing that is *not* preserved is the thing this was for: the image
content.
